summary: A volcanic island nation in the North Atlantic, settled by Nordic Vikings in the 9th century. The Althing, established in 930, is regarded as one of the oldest parliaments, and the country is known for glaciers, hot springs and the aurora.

ranking.name: Church of Iceland (Lutheran)
ranking.description: In 1550 the Danish ruler forced Iceland to convert to Lutheranism and executed the Catholic bishop Jón Arason; after that the Church of Iceland became the state church, guaranteed by the constitution, with church taxes collected by the government. In the past almost everyone was automatically registered as a member at birth, hence the high share; but it was about 90 percent in the 1990s and has recently fallen to about half, and most people do not attend church regularly.

ranking.name: No religion or unregistered
ranking.description: Iceland is one of the fastest-secularizing countries in the Nordic region. With high educational attainment, urbanization, and falling trust in traditional institutions around the 2008 financial crisis, more and more people have left the state church. Since 2013 newborns are no longer automatically registered with the state church along with their mother, so the number of people unregistered or registered as non-religious has grown rapidly.

ranking.name: Other Lutheran free churches
ranking.description: From the late 19th century some believers, dissatisfied with the choice of local pastors or the administration of the state church, formed free churches of their own, such as the free churches of Reykjavik and Hafnarfjörður. Theologically they are still Lutheran, but are financially and organizationally independent of the state church.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: After the Reformation of 1550, Catholicism almost disappeared from Iceland, and the church was re-established only in the late 19th century by missionaries from France and elsewhere. Recent growth has come mainly from immigrants from Poland, the Philippines and other countries after 2004, so Catholicism is the largest religion among Iceland's immigrant communities.

ranking.name: Old Norse faith (Ásatrú)
ranking.description: Ásatrú is a neo-pagan movement reviving the Norse faith of the Viking Age; it was founded in 1972 by the poet Sveinbjörn Beinteinsson and officially recognized the following year. Icelanders feel a strong identification with their sagas and Viking ancestors, which has attracted a certain number of followers at home, and Reykjavik is building the first Norse temple in 1,000 years.

religion.background: Iceland was settled by Norwegians in the late 9th century, who at first followed Norse polytheism. Around the year 1000, the Icelandic parliament (Althing), under pressure from the Norwegian king, resolved that the whole country accept Christianity, while permitting private worship of the old gods. In 1550 the Danish king forced through the Lutheran Reformation, executing the last Catholic bishop, Jón Arason, and Lutheranism has been the state religion ever since. From the late 20th century Iceland has secularized rapidly, with membership of the state church declining year by year, and in 1972 the Old Norse faith also gained official recognition.

ranking.name: Icelandic
ranking.description: Icelandic descends directly from the Old Norse of the 9th-century Viking settlers, and because of geographic isolation has preserved archaic grammar and vocabulary. The independence movement of the 19th century regarded Icelandic as the core of national identity; after independence it became the sole national language, used in schools, government and the media, and a 2011 law formally confirmed its official status.

ranking.name: Polish
ranking.description: After the EU's eastern enlargement in 2004, Poles moved to Iceland in large numbers to meet the labor demand of the construction industry, fish processing and aluminum smelters, and Poles became Iceland's largest foreign community. Some returned home during the 2008 financial crisis, but the later boom in tourism attracted more, so Polish has become the second most common native language in Iceland.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: Icelanders learn English at school from childhood, and with English-language film and television, the internet and millions of tourists every year, most Icelanders speak English fluently, though few have it as a native language. The strength of English has also raised concern in the Icelandic government about the "digital extinction" of the language, and in recent years it has invested funds in developing speech and AI technology for Icelandic.

language.history: Icelandic derives from the Old Norse brought by Norwegian settlers in the 9th century. Because Iceland is isolated in the North Atlantic, the language has changed very little, and modern Icelanders can still roughly read the sagas of the 12th–13th centuries. During Danish rule (1380–1944) Danish dominated commerce and administration, but the national movement of the 19th century promoted "linguistic purism", creating new words from native Icelandic roots to replace loanwords. After independence in 1944, the Icelandic Language Committee has continued to coin native words for new things such as computers and telephones; for example, the computer is called tölva (number + prophetess).

ranking.name: Skyr (Icelandic yogurt)
ranking.description: A thick dairy product made by fermenting skim milk and straining off the whey; its texture is like yogurt, but it is high in protein and slightly sour. It is often eaten for breakfast or dessert with blueberries, or with milk and sugar.
ranking.history: The method of making skyr was very likely brought to Iceland by Norwegian settlers in the 9th–10th centuries, and it is already mentioned in medieval saga literature. Other parts of the Nordic region later stopped making it, but in Iceland the cold climate and pastoral economy kept it going, and it became an important winter source of protein. In the late 20th century Icelandic dairy companies commercialized it, and in recent years it has been marketed in the United States and Europe, becoming a representative Icelandic food.

ranking.name: Smoked lamb (hangikjöt)
ranking.description: Lamb smoked over birch wood or dried sheep dung, usually boiled and sliced, and eaten with potatoes in white sauce and green peas. It has a strong smoky aroma and saltiness, and can be eaten hot or cold.
ranking.history: Hangikjöt means "hung meat", because traditionally lamb was hung in the chimney or smokehouse of a farmhouse to be smoked and preserved. Trees are scarce in Iceland, so people smoked meat with sheep dung, a practice adapted to a land without forests. It is the most important traditional dish at Icelandic Christmas, and is often served with flatbread and red cabbage.

ranking.name: Fermented shark (hákarl)
ranking.description: Greenland shark meat is buried in gravel to ferment for several weeks, then hung to air-dry for four to five months, and eaten in small pieces; it has a pungent ammonia taste.
ranking.history: The fresh meat of the Greenland shark contains large amounts of urea and trimethylamine oxide and is toxic, but early Icelanders discovered that after fermentation and drying it could be eaten safely. This preservation method let islanders short of food make use of precious protein. Today it is eaten mainly at the winter festival Þorrablót together with other traditional foods, often with a swig of the Icelandic spirit Brennivín.

ranking.name: Icelandic flatbread (flatkaka)
ranking.description: A round unleavened thin bread made from rye flour, traditionally baked directly on hot coals to leave scorch marks, often spread with butter and served with smoked lamb. It is chewy with a slightly toasty aroma, and often cut into small wedges.
ranking.history: Iceland's climate is cold and wheat is hard to grow, so historically flour mostly had to be imported from Denmark, and bread used to be a precious food. Flatkaka needs no yeast and can be made with only a little rye flour, so it is a frugal household bread. Today it is often paired with slices of hangikjöt or smoked salmon as a snack, and is also a traditional food on the festive tables of Christmas and Þorrablót.

ranking.name: Dried fish (harðfiskur)
ranking.description: Dried fish made by air-drying cod or wolffish in cold wind for several months, usually spread with butter and eaten as a snack. Its texture is dry, hard and chewy, rich in protein, and it can be torn off and eaten as is.
ranking.history: Iceland has lived by fishing since the Middle Ages, and fish dried in the cold, dry sea wind keeps for years; it was an important staple of the early Icelanders, and dried cod was also a major export commodity to Europe from the 14th century. In the past Icelanders often ate dried fish as bread, while today it is a high-protein snack available in supermarkets and at gas stations.
